profiled_workloads.selection_reason: Lowest eval speedup (0.572x) and highest eval latency (92.17 us) of the round: the worst regime must be explained first.
Second-lowest speedup (0.710x) at the same [4096,4096] element count as the fp16 control; isolates the dtype-dependent compute path.
Strong control: identical numel and byte volume to selu_-timing-7 but fp16 dtype, and the only large-case workload already above 1.0x.
Representative of the nine small (1024-1048576 element) workloads that carry most of the geo_mean weight and are the target of the frozen host-launch hypothesis.

findings.label: Small workloads: >=87% of eval walltime is outside the profiled device kernel

evidence.metric: Task Duration(us) avg over 100 invocations (_selu_nomask, Block Num 1)
consecutive kernel start-to-start gap in the profiled loop (tasks 1->2->3), dominant ~20 us cluster

findings.inference: The profiled device task for the 1024-element fp16 case is 1.652 us (min 1.14), while this round's eval walltime is 12.848 us, so at most ~13% of measured call time is device work; the dominant start-to-start cluster of ~20 us inside the instrumented loop shows the submission path, not the kernel, paces iteration. This corroborates the frozen hypothesis that the nine small workloads are host-launch bound, and round 2 moved the headline metric in the right direction on them (-0.32 us mean eval latency, 0.795x -> 0.916x, geo_mean +7.1%). It also bounds the remaining headroom: PyTorch's reference is 11.773 us for the same call, so only ~1.1 us of the gap is still attributable to the candidate's own launch path, and the floor is set by harness-plus-launch cost common to both. Profiling inflates host time, so the 20 us gap is diagnostic ordering evidence, not an eval-scale measurement.

findings.label: Large bf16: vector pipe is 2.08x the fp16 control at identical byte volume; the fp32 upcast branch is the mechanism

evidence.metric: aiv_vec_ratio (vector share of aiv_time) for bf16
aiv_vec_time(us) for the fp16 control, same 16777216 elements
aiv_mte2_time(us) bf16 vs fp16 (identical 2-byte element count)
Block Num (program count) bf16 vs fp16

findings.inference: bf16 (83.544 us device) and fp16 (45.860 us device) move the same interface byte volume, so the 1.82x device-time gap cannot be transfer; it is the vector pipe, whose time is 2.08x (56.66 vs 27.21 us) and whose share rises to 66-68% of aiv_time. The candidate source routes every non-fp16 dtype through the fp32 upcast branch (lines 35-37: x.to(tl.float32), exp in fp32, y.to(dtype)), while fp16 uses the native-precision branch (lines 33-34). Measured per-element vector cost is 3.38 us/M-element for bf16 versus 2.76 for fp32 (46.29 us) and 1.62 for fp16, i.e. bf16 is the most expensive despite having half of fp32's bytes, which is consistent with paying two full-vector dtype conversions on top of fp32 exp. Vector time is stable to <0.01 us across invocations, so this is a codegen property of the dtype path, not run-to-run noise. Caveat: the instruction listing that would prove the cast sequence was cancelled, so the cast attribution is source-plus-metric inference, not SASS evidence.

findings.label: Large fp32: device task is 1.57x the reference-side device time and is vector-dominated, not transfer-dominated

evidence.metric: aiv_vec_time(us) per invocation (46.29 / 46.296 steady) vs aiv_time(us) 81.185

findings.inference: The profiled device task (82.78 us) already accounts for most of the 92.17 us eval latency against a 52.68 us reference, so the loss is inside the kernel, not in launch. Vector time 46.29 us dominates aiv_time 81.19 us, while both transfer pipes together are only ~29 us; with the reference also running vector math on the same 134 MB in-place traffic, the gap to 52.68 us is more plausibly vector-instruction efficiency and per-program fixed cost than bandwidth saturation. fp32's 1e-4 tolerance forbids the reduced-precision treatment that is plausible for bf16, so this regime needs an instruction-level look (cast/exp expansion, loop structure) before any edit; no such artifact exists this round.

findings.label: Per-program fixed cost is ~5.5 ns and explains the scalar-time spread between the 1024- and 2048-program regimes

evidence.metric: aiv_scalar_time(us) bf16 vs fp32 steady state
aiv_scalar_time(us) for fp32 with Block Num 2048 (BLOCK 8192), versus 5.635 us at Block Num 1024 for fp16 (BLOCK 16384)

findings.inference: _pick_block gives non-fp16 dtypes half the tile (8192) and therefore twice the programs (2048 vs 1024) on the same numel; scalar time tracks program count at a stable ~5.4 ns/program across all three dtypes, contributing ~5.5 us of the deficit for bf16/fp32 relative to fp16. This is a real but secondary lever: it is smaller than the ~29 us vector gap, and raising the tile to 16384 for bf16/fp32 is blocked by the recorded UB requirement (2,097,408 bits needed vs 1,572,864 available) plus prior no-gain persistent-loop records, so it is not the recommended first move.

performance_interpretation: Round 2 improved geo_mean 0.8252 -> 0.8839 (+7.1%) and the evidence splits the twelve timing workloads into two regimes rather than one bound. Nine small workloads (1024-1048576 elements) carry only ~1.2-1.8 us of device work against ~12.4-13.4 us eval walltime, so they are launch/latency bound; the round-2 host-path change is the reason those cases moved from ~0.79-0.93x to ~0.87-1.09x, and only ~1.1 us remains before they match PyTorch's ~10.8-11.8 us floor. Three [4096,4096] workloads are device bound and are where the remaining losses sit: fp16 is already 1.248x (device 45.86 us, vector 27.21 us), bf16 is 0.710x (device 83.54 us, vector 56.66 us at the same bytes), fp32 is 0.572x (device 82.78 us, vector 46.29 us against a 52.68 us reference). bf16 is the clearest defect: it moves half of fp32's bytes yet costs the same total device time, and its per-element vector cost (3.38 us/M-element) exceeds both fp32 (2.76) and fp16 (1.62) because the non-fp16 branch forces an fp32 upcast/downcast around the exponential. msprof timings above are diagnostic; all speedups and latencies are the round-2 eval values.

next_experiment.action_description: Give bf16 its own kernel branch instead of reusing the fp32 upcast branch: keep the positive-side select exactly in native bf16, but evaluate the exponential through fp16 precision - cast the negative-side operand to fp16, apply exp, then form lambda*alpha*(e-1) and store in bf16. Leave the fp16 branch (source line 33) and the fp32 branch (lines 36-37) semantically untouched, and apply the same branch to _selu_masked and _selu_strided so all three kernels stay consistent. The strided/masked paths and the host dispatch table are not otherwise changed.
next_experiment.expected_impact: Targets selu_-timing-7 only: predicted vector time 56.66 us -> 27-40 us and aiv_time 83.25 us -> ~55-65 us, so device task 83.5 us -> 55-65 us and eval speedup 0.710x -> 0.90-1.05x. That alone is worth roughly +3% to +4% on geo_mean (0.884 -> ~0.91-0.92) if the other eleven workloads hold. If vector time stays near 56.7 us after the change, the cast/precision hypothesis is refuted and the bf16 cost must lie elsewhere (tile geometry or exp lowering).
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: Precision risk is bounded but real: fp16 has a 10-bit mantissa and its range only affects the branch where exp is taken (x<0 gives exp in (0,1]), so negative inputs saturate to -1.758 which is the correct limit, and positives are returned from the untouched bf16 operand. The bf16 correctness cases already show 0.03-0.06 relative-error observations against a 1.5% tolerance, so any precision change must be accepted by the full correctness set, not by inspection. Do not touch the fp32 branch: its 1e-4 tolerance does not permit this treatment. Rollback is a one-line revert of the bf16 branch to the fp32 path; if fp16 codegen expands exp16 back to fp32 (no vector-time drop) or the bf16 correctness set regresses, revert and re-profile rather than layering further precision experiments.
success_criteria: All 24 correctness workloads PASS (three dtypes, strided and contiguous, including empty and 1025-element cases) plus the batch's extra dense-pointwise semantic checks; no correctness case may be dropped to make the headline metric.

Profiled aiv_vec_time for selu_-timing-7 falls from 56.66 us to <=40 us and aiv_time from 83.25 us to <=65 us, with the change in the same direction as the eval latency (falsifies the cast/precision hypothesis if vector time is unchanged).
selu_-timing-7 eval latency <=65 us and eval speedup >=0.90x, up from 0.710x.

Guard workloads do not regress: selu_-timing-3 (fp16 control) and selu_-timing-11 (fp32) stay within +/-2% of 45.60 us and 92.17 us, and the small host-bound cases (selu_-timing-6 representative) stay within +/-2%.
Full-eval headline geo_mean > 0.8839 (round-2 value) with the same twelve timing workloads; target >=0.91.

warnings: The instruction-level collection requested for selu_-timing-7 and selu_-timing-3 was cancelled by the client (status RUN_CANCELLED, reason_code server_operation_cancelled) before any instruction artifact was persisted, so no SASS/simulator evidence exists for this round; the bf16 cast mechanism is source-plus-metric inference only.
All timings from msprof are diagnostic and are not eval latency; eval speedups, latencies and deltas are the round-2 values from get_profile_context.

Pipeline-active ratios are marginal statistics that can overlap and must not be summed into a time decomposition; no quantitative Roofline claim is made because no calibrated hardware limit or physical-byte counter was collected.

Both large non-fp16 workloads use BLOCK=8192 (2048 programs) while fp16 uses 16384 (1024 programs); cross-dtype comparisons hold element count and byte volume fixed but not program geometry, so the ~5.5 us scalar difference is attributed to program count and not to arithmetic.
open_questions: Which instruction sequence implements the bf16 path (two full-vector conversions vs a fused cast/exp), and whether the fp32 exp expands to a multi-instruction polynomial that a different formulation could shorten.
Why the round-2 host-path change produced only ~0.3 us of the remaining ~1.1 us gap to PyTorch on small cases, and what share of the ~10-11 us common floor is harness-versus-launch cost.
Whether the bf16/fp32 tile can be raised toward 16384 by shortening intermediate lifetimes, given the recorded 2,097,408-bit UB requirement at that tile.
Whether the round-2 regression on selu_-timing-11 (+11.5% latency) and the stagnation of selu_-timing-7 are run-to-run variance or a real cost of the new host path.
